title: Common Network Attacks
summary: The attack patterns interviewers ask you to name and explain at the network/transport level — MITM, spoofing, floods, and amplification.

slides.markdown:
A **MITM** attack sits an attacker between two parties who believe they're talking directly, silently reading or altering traffic. The pattern is generic — link layer (ARP spoofing), DNS layer, or application layer (a fake Wi-Fi hotspot).

Encryption alone doesn't solve this: **without authentication**, the attacker's own key just gets used instead of the real server's — securely talking to the wrong party. That's why TLS certificates verify identity, not just scramble bytes.

assets.alt: Man-in-the-middle attacker intercepting traffic between two parties

slides.sectionTitle: ARP spoofing as a MITM vector
slides.markdown:
ARP has no authentication — any host on a LAN can claim to own any IP address, and other hosts will believe it. An attacker sends forged ARP replies claiming to be the default gateway, so victims send their traffic to the attacker instead, who forwards it on (invisibly) after reading or altering it.

This works specifically because it's a local-network attack — the attacker must be on the same LAN segment. See [ARP & Address Resolution](arp-address-resolution) for the full mechanism.

Rather than intercepting traffic directly, DNS-layer attacks corrupt the *map* itself: a forged DNS response tells a victim (or a whole resolver's cache) that a legitimate hostname resolves to an attacker-controlled IP.

Once poisoned, everyone using that resolver gets redirected until the bad entry's TTL expires or it's manually flushed — a single successful poisoning can silently redirect many victims at once. See [DNS: Domain Name Resolution](dns-resolution).

A **SYN flood** attacks the TCP handshake directly: a stream of `SYN` packets (often spoofed source IPs) each claim a slot in the server's connection backlog, but the final `ACK` never arrives to complete any of them.

Enough half-open connections exhaust the backlog queue, and the server can no longer accept handshakes from legitimate clients — denial of service without ever sending a byte of real traffic. See [TCP Connection Setup & Teardown](tcp-connection-management).

| | DoS | DDoS |
|---|---|---|
| Source | Single machine/connection | Many machines (often a botnet) |
| Blocking by IP | Often works | Rarely helps — thousands of distinct sources |
| Typical scale | Limited by one attacker's bandwidth | Can reach terabits/sec |

The "distributed" in DDoS is the actual defensive problem: you can't just block one bad IP when the traffic is arriving from thousands of them simultaneously.

The attacker sends a small request to a third-party server (like an open DNS or NTP resolver) with the victim's IP **spoofed as the source** — the server dutifully sends its (often much larger) response to the victim instead of the real requester.

Certain protocols make excellent amplifiers because a tiny request yields a disproportionately large response — a small DNS query can trigger a response tens of times its size, letting an attacker with modest bandwidth generate a flood far exceeding what they could send directly.

Anyone with access to the traffic's path — a shared Wi-Fi network, a compromised router, an ISP — can passively capture and read **plaintext** traffic with tools like Wireshark. No active interference needed; just listening is enough.

This is the concrete, everyday reason "HTTPS everywhere" matters: encryption turns a trivially readable stream into ciphertext, closing off passive sniffing as an attack vector entirely, without requiring the victim to do anything differently.

**IP spoofing** means forging the source address field in a packet's IP header — the sender claims to be someone else. It's the enabling technique behind both SYN floods (hiding the real attacker, complicating blocking) and amplification attacks (redirecting responses to a victim).

Networks can partially defend against this with **ingress/egress filtering** (BCP 38) — an ISP refusing to forward packets whose source address couldn't plausibly have originated from that network segment — though adoption is inconsistent across the internet.

Attacker → spoofed request (victim's IP as source) → open DNS/NTP server → large response → victim, overwhelmed. The attacker never directly touches the victim; the amplifying server does the flooding on their behalf, unwittingly.

The victim's only visible traffic is a flood of unsolicited responses *from legitimate-looking DNS/NTP servers* — which is what makes this class of attack so effective at hiding the true source.

assets.alt: Reflection and amplification attack flow via a spoofed third-party server

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: where each attack sits in the stack
slides.markdown:
| Layer | Attack |
|---|---|
| Link | ARP spoofing |
| Network | IP spoofing |
| Transport | SYN flood |
| Application/DNS | DNS spoofing/cache poisoning |

Knowing the layer tells you where a defense must live — link-layer attacks need switch-port security, transport-layer floods need SYN cookies or rate limiting, application attacks need DNSSEC or resolver hardening.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a firewall alone stops DDoS
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We have a firewall, so a DDoS attack will be blocked."

**Why it's wrong:** a firewall filters traffic by rules — but a **volumetric** DDoS doesn't need to get *past* the firewall; it just needs to saturate the network link or overwhelm the firewall's own capacity before traffic reaches your application logic.

**Correct model:** volumetric attacks need volumetric defenses — upstream scrubbing, anycast distribution, ISP-level capacity — not just edge rules. A firewall handles targeted attacks; it isn't built for raw bandwidth floods.
